austagram-paneer.desc: Cattle and buffalo graze on haor grass around Austagram for most of the year, and their creamy milk has long been turned into paneer here. Local accounts trace the craft back about 300 years to the Mughal period, starting with a few families in Dattapara. Milk is curdled, strained through cloth and pressed into bamboo baskets, giving a firm white cheese with a mild salty tang. It takes about ten kilos of milk for a kilo, so it is not cheap, and most of it goes to Dhaka, Sylhet and Kishoreganj.

glance: 100 km to Kishoreganj by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
itna-mithamoin-austagram-road.desc: Opened in 2020, this road runs for about 30 km across the deep haor, linking Itna, Mithamoin and Austagram upazilas. In the monsoon it seems to float, with nothing but water to the horizon, while in winter the land around it is green paddy. Travellers ride motorbikes, autos and bicycles along it simply for the view. Raised bridges let water and boats pass underneath.
blocks: How to get there
From Kishoreganj town head via Karimganj towards Mithamoin; routes change with the water level, so ask locally whether to go by road or by boat from Chamraghat.
Good to know
Stopping is easy, but watch for fast motorbikes; sunrise and sunset are best.

glance: 100 km to Kishoreganj by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
egarosindur-shah-mahmud-mosque.desc: Egarosindur in Pakundia upazila was once a river trading town and a stronghold of Isa Khan, the Baro Bhuiyan leader who fought the Mughals; it is mentioned in the Akbarnama. Little of the fort remains above ground, but the village keeps two old mosques. The Shah Mahmud Mosque is a square, single-domed brick building with octagonal corner towers, entered through a small gatehouse with a curved do-chala roof, and bits of terracotta still show on its walls. The smaller Sadi Mosque of the 1650s stands a few hundred metres away, and an old dighi lies nearby.
blocks: How to get there
Bus or CNG from Kishoreganj town to Pakundia, then a CNG or auto to Egarosindur village (about 8 km from the upazila centre).
Good to know
Both mosques are in use for prayers, so visit outside prayer times and dress modestly. Ask locals for the Sadi Mosque, which is easy to miss.

glance: 100 km to Kishoreganj by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
qutub-shah-mosque-austagram.desc: Out in Austagram, where the haor stretches to the horizon in the rains, stands the Qutub Shah Mosque, thought to date from the late Sultanate period of the 16th century. It has a large central dome flanked by two smaller domes on each side, octagonal corner towers, and traces of terracotta in its mihrabs and facade. A grave beside it is said to belong to the saint Qutub Shah, after whom it is named. It is a protected monument and fits naturally into a trip along the Itna–Mithamoin–Austagram road.
blocks: How to get there
From Kishoreganj go to Chamraghat or Bhairab and take a boat to Austagram in the rainy season; in the dry season use the haor road. From Austagram sadar the mosque is a short auto or walk.
Good to know
Combine it with a haor boat trip. It is an active mosque, so avoid prayer times.

guroi-shahi-mosque.desc: In Guroi village of Nikli upazila stands an old square mosque with a large bulb-shaped dome and four octagonal corner minarets. A long, narrow inscription at the base of the dome is read as dating it to around 1680, and the building mixes Mughal and earlier Sultanate features; locals claim it is much older. Its western wall has three mihrabs, the central one larger. Few of the visitors who come to Nikli for the haor know it is there.
blocks: How to get there
From Nikli upazila town take an auto or, in the rainy season, a boat to Guroi village.
Good to know
Pair it with a boat ride on Nikli Haor. It is an active mosque, so visit outside prayer times.

glance: 100 km to Kishoreganj by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
chandrabati-shiva-temple.desc: Chandrabati lived in the 16th century in Patuabhanga village near Kishoreganj town and is widely regarded as the first woman poet in the Bengali language. Her retelling of the Ramayana and the tragic ballads tied to her life form part of the Mymensingh Gitika. A small, tall Shiva temple said to have been built by her father Dwija Bangshidas still stands near her home site. It is a quiet, moving place for anyone interested in Bengali literature.
blocks: How to get there
Auto or CNG from Kishoreganj town to Patuabhanga, about 20–30 minutes.

glance: 100 km to Kishoreganj by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
jangalbari-fort.desc: Isa Khan, who led the Baro Bhuiyans against Mughal expansion in the late 16th century, held a fortified base at Jangalbari in Karimganj upazila. Today you can see parts of the moat and earthen walls, a small mosque and the house of his descendants. It is a modest site, but the history attached to it is significant. Few visitors make the trip, so locals are often happy to show you around.
blocks: How to get there
CNG from Kishoreganj town to Karimganj and on to Jangalbari, about 30–40 minutes.
Good to know
Part of the site is a private home; ask before entering.

glance: 100 km to Kishoreganj by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
nikli-haor.desc: Nikli is the most accessible of Kishoreganj's haors and a favourite weekend trip from Dhaka. In the rainy months the low basin fills completely, and the Nikli embankment becomes a long promenade with water on both sides. Trawlers and small boats take visitors out to village islands, where houses sit on raised mounds. At sunset the water and sky blur together.
blocks: How to get there
Bus from Dhaka to Kishoreganj town, then a CNG or local bus to Nikli, about 1 hour.
Good to know
Wear life jackets on boats and avoid going out in storms; carry rain gear.

glance: 100 km to Kishoreganj by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
pagla-mosque-kishoreganj.desc: Pagla Mosque stands on the Narasunda river in Kishoreganj town. Its fame comes from the belief that wishes made here are granted, so people of many faiths leave cash, gold and even livestock in its donation boxes. When the boxes are opened every few months, counting the money makes national news. It is worth a short stop to see the crowds and the riverside setting.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw from anywhere in Kishoreganj town.
Good to know
Dress modestly and avoid prayer times.

glance: 100 km to Kishoreganj by road, 3–4 hours by bus or car
shahidi-mosque-kishoreganj.desc: After the famous Pagla Mosque, the Shahidi Masjid is the best-known mosque in Kishoreganj. It stands in the heart of the district town, a three-storey building with a single tall minaret about as high as a five-storey block. Around it runs a Qawmi madrasa, Al-Jamiatul Imdadia. The great Sholakia Eidgah, home of the country's largest Eid congregation, is a short distance away, so the two are easy to see together.
blocks: How to get there
Any rickshaw or auto in Kishoreganj town can take you there; it is in the town centre.
Good to know
Visit outside prayer times and dress modestly. Walk on to Sholakia Eidgah afterwards; on Eid morning the whole area fills with worshippers.

sholakia-eid.desc: Sholakia Eidgah, on the edge of Kishoreganj town, hosts the biggest Eid prayer congregation in Bangladesh, with hundreds of thousands of worshippers on Eid ul-Fitr. People travel from across the country, and special trains run from Dhaka. The prayer begins with the firing of a gun as a signal, an old local custom. Even watching from the edge, the sea of people is a remarkable sight.
blocks: Good to know
Arrive very early, expect heavy security and crowds, and dress for prayer if attending.

glance: Local eateries at Nikli bazar and the haor ghats
kishoreganj-haor-fish.desc: The haors are among the richest freshwater fisheries in Bangladesh, and fish is the centre of every meal here. Big catfish like boal and ayre are cooked in spicy curries, while small fish such as mola and puti are fried or made into a light jhol. Fish markets in Bhairab, Nikli and Kishoreganj town are lively in the morning. Ask your boatman or homestay to cook the day's catch.

glance: Bazaar eateries in Nikli, Itna and Mithamoin
kishoreganj-haor-duck.desc: Large flocks of ducks are herded across the haors, feeding on snails and fish in the shallow water. Their meat is darker and richer than chicken, and locals cook it slowly with plenty of garlic, ginger and spices. In winter it is often eaten with chitoi pitha or flat rice cakes. Duck eggs from the haor are also sold at bazaars across the region.
